# 2. Course purpose

The course develops a working understanding of molecular biology and its use in
ecological and evolutionary research. Students move from the molecular basis of
information to a defensible study design:

**biological question → sample → molecule → assay → sequence or measurement → computation → inference**

Cox, *Molecular Biology: Principles and Practice*, 2nd ed. (2015), provides the
foundation for the opening weeks and a reference throughout the course. Method
chapters and primary literature supply the case studies; the full list is on the
[materials page](materials.qmd).

# 3. Course aims

After completing the course, students should:

1. understand the molecular principles behind DNA, RNA, proteins, genomes, gene expression, and molecular phenotypes;
2. understand the strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate uses of major molecular methods in ecology and evolutionary biology;
3. develop practical competence in sample design, nucleic-acid extraction, quantification, PCR, electrophoresis, sequencing, and basic computational analysis;
4. learn to connect molecular observations with ecological interactions, population structure, phylogeny, and environmental change;
5. develop reproducible habits for controls, contamination prevention, metadata, quality assessment, and scientific reporting;
6. design an end-to-end molecular study and defend the limitations of the proposed inference.

# 4. Learning outcomes

On successful completion, students can:

- explain the chemical and informational basis of nucleic acids and proteins;
- explain replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, translation, RNA processing, and regulation;
- choose sampling and preservation strategies for environmental, tissue, faecal, sediment, or low-biomass material;
- design extraction and amplification workflows with appropriate blanks, positive controls, negative controls, technical replicates, and inhibition checks;
- interpret agarose gels, Sanger traces, qPCR curves, standard curves, FASTQ quality metrics, and Nanopore run reports;
- compare Sanger, short-read, and long-read sequencing for a stated biological objective;
- use marker genes, metabarcoding, genome comparisons, phylogenetic analyses, and population-genetic summaries appropriately;
- interpret selected transcriptomic, proteomic, hybridization, microscopy, and flow-cytometry evidence;
- connect molecular observations to species interactions, symbiosis, population processes, and environmental monitoring;
- produce a reproducible report that distinguishes observation, analysis, inference, and speculation.

# 5. Course content

The four blocks are expanded, with the methods each one covers, on the
[topics page](topics.qmd).

### Block I — Foundations and measurement

- evolution, scientific reasoning, and molecular biology as a way of knowing;
- chemical properties of DNA, RNA, proteins, buffers, enzymes, and molecular interactions;
- information flow, replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, translation, and regulation;
- sample representativeness, preservation, extraction, quantification, inhibition, and contamination.

### Block II — The molecular toolkit

- electrophoresis, restriction analysis, Southern blotting, PCR, qPCR, ddPCR, Sanger sequencing, probes, FISH, fluorescence, and flow cytometry;
- molecular markers, barcoding, metabarcoding, allozymes, RFLP, microsatellites, and SNPs;
- Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, library preparation, read quality, assembly, annotation, and data management.

### Block III — Genomes and molecular phenotypes

- comparative genomics, assembly, annotation, and public sequence databases;
- transcriptomics, non-coding RNA, condition- and stage-specific regulation, epigenetics, and functional genomics;
- proteomics, quantitative proteomics, protein interactions, post-translational modification, and molecular phenotypes;
- the cell biology behind the traits we measure: life-cycle stages, secretion, transport, and cellular responses to the environment.

### Block IV — Ecology, evolution, and application

- phylogeny, phylogeography, population genetics, coalescence, and community-level inference;
- species interactions, symbiosis, host-associated microbiota, and environmental monitoring;
- CRISPR, LAMP, microfluidics, lab-on-chip, biosensing, and field-deployable diagnostics;

# 6. Textbook architecture

**Cox — molecular foundation**

- Ch. 1: evolution and scientific reasoning;
- Ch. 2–8: DNA, RNA, proteins, genes, genomes, transcriptomes, and proteomes;
- Ch. 11–18: replication, mutation, repair, recombination, transcription, RNA processing, translation, and genetic manipulation;
- Ch. 19–22: regulation of gene expression.

Book examples are used to demonstrate how methods answer biological questions.
Students are not expected to read all chapters cover-to-cover. Textbook figures
should be linked or used under the relevant institutional permissions; teaching
diagrams should otherwise be redrawn as original explanatory figures.

# 7. Teaching and learning methods

- short lectures followed by structured interpretation of a figure, dataset, or method decision;
- small-group [seminars](seminars/index.qmd) based on one paper, figure, or case study;
- wet-lab practicals using approved teaching material and non-pathogenic controls;
- virtual PCR/qPCR and sequence-analysis exercises;
- public sequence, genome, and biodiversity databases with open computational tools;

# 8. Assessment

The course is graded A–F on three components, and all three have to be there.

| Component | Weight | How it is judged |
|---|---:|---|
| Seminar presentation | 25% | Pass / no pass — one research article, presented to the group in week 13 |
| Practical laboratory work | 25% | The three laboratory sessions in weeks 14–16 and the work handed in from them |
| Oral examination | 50% | A conversation about the course material, in the examination period |

### The seminar is pass or no pass

There is no scale and no rubric score behind this 25%: you either present a
paper and show that you understood how its evidence was produced, or you do
not. A presentation that falls short can be repeated once. What makes a good
one, and the registration form, are on the [seminars page](seminars/index.qmd).

### The practicals are the bench work

The last three sessions of the semester are laboratory sessions, running the
chain the whole course has been describing — sampling and extraction, then
amplification and sequencing, then the analysis and the write-up. They are
assessed together, on what you did at the bench and what you made of the result:
controls run, deviations recorded, numbers interpreted honestly.

Attendance at the practicals is not optional in the way a lecture is. A session
you miss has to be made up, and the laboratory safety induction has to be done
before you can be in the room at all.

### The oral examination is scaled to what you already did

The examination is a conversation, and how long a conversation depends on the
record you bring to it.

- **You attended, presented, and did the practical work.** The examination is a
  short discussion of what you found interesting and what you would do
  differently — a confirmation, not an interrogation.
- **You have gaps.** The examination covers the topics of the sessions you
  missed and the work you did not finish. Nothing exotic: the material of those
  weeks, at the level it was taught.

That is the entire reason attendance is recorded. It is not a compliance
exercise — it is the thing the examination is measured against, and it is kept
in the open where you can check it yourself through the
[participation tracker](participation.qmd).

# 9. Biosafety and ethical practice

The course does not require culturing pathogenic organisms. Teaching activities
use non-pathogenic organisms, preserved material, purified DNA/RNA, commercial
controls, prepared images, or public datasets. Any live work must follow
institutional biosafety, waste, ethics, and sample-transfer procedures.

Students must record sample origin, collection date, preservation, extraction
batch, control status, software version, parameter choices, and any deviation
from the planned workflow.

# 10. Workload model

The semester is sixteen weekly sessions:

| Activity | Sessions | When |
|---|---:|---|
| Lectures and demonstrations | 12 | Weeks 1–12 |
| Student seminar presentations | 1 | Week 13 |
| Practical laboratories | 3 | Weeks 14–16 |
| Oral examination | — | Examination period |

Independent work is the reading for each lecture, the preparation of one seminar
paper, and the write-up of the practicals. The hour split behind these sessions
follows whichever credit volume is approved; the totals proposed for the
expanded version are in section 1.

# 11. Administrative implementation note {#implementation-note}

The existing 6 ECTS course can be retained as a compact version by selecting
weeks 1–8 and 12, keeping the seminar, and reducing the practical block from
three sessions to one. The 10 ECTS version should be adopted only after the
timetable, laboratory capacity, staffing, assessment load, and programme-level
credit requirements have been confirmed.
